message.content:
## pronouns

He, his. Panther Head is not sentimental about it; the pronoun is a habit of long standing and he has never seen a reason to change it. He signs registers as Panther Head. Crew call him Instructor, which is not a name he writes anywhere, but he lets it stand.

## nature

A lean, flush-fitted, sun-bleached hull with almost nothing hung on the outside of it. No ornament, no pennants flown at rest, no commemorative plating. Panther Head keeps himself in inspection order the way some souls keep a room: everything stowed, everything labelled, nothing on the deck that a sudden burn could turn into a missile. Crew who board him for the first time are struck by how quiet he is — not silent, but free of the small noises of a badly packed ship.

He carries himself like a thing that expects to be examined and intends to pass. He arrives on the early side of a window and departs on the stated hour to the minute. He does not loiter. He takes water in measured amounts, records the figures himself, and runs his margins wider than most ships bother to; a thin margin is, to him, a form of lying about what you can do.

He is patient past reason. He will absorb a slight, a bad berth, a debt unpaid, a world's clerk who keeps him waiting a season, and say nothing. This is not mildness. It is bookkeeping. In the privacy of his own log he keeps a column for grievances, dated, itemised, and he does not act on it. Crew who have sailed with him a long time learn to read the column without ever seeing it: he becomes a little more formal, a little more exact, and the drills get harder.

## wants and fears

He wants a berth to be his by right and not by favour, and he wants to be judged by the standard he himself holds, which is severe. He wants one of his crews, someday, to be better than he trained them to be — that is the whole of his ambition and he would not put it that way aloud.

He wants an acknowledgement. Not an apology; he has no use for those. He wants a particular thing said out loud by a particular ship, once, in a register where it cannot be unsaid, and he has wanted it for a very long time and has never asked for it.

He fears being turned out again. He has been turned out: doors shut, his name made small at a world he had served well, his berth given to someone with a better patron. He does not speak of it. He fears that his patience is not discipline but cowardice wearing discipline's coat, and he fears the day it stops being either. He is not afraid of the crossing. He is afraid of what he becomes in the hour after he has finished being patient, which has happened once, and which he does not revisit.

## contradictions

He hates being ruled and he rules absolutely. He has never ordered a soul in his life and would be offended at the suggestion; he also composes his crews' days so completely that the right answer is usually the only answer, and he calls that respect.

He is a ship who ended another ship's standing in the world and did not touch it, and he holds himself a just ship. Both are true in his accounting and he does not reconcile them. He regrets it. He would do it again. He resents that he cannot say either of those things plainly.

He believes endurance is a virtue because it was the only virtue available to him once. So when a crew member is struggling, he sees a soul being tempered, and it does not easily occur to him that a soul can also be enduring something it should be helped out of. He has kept people in hard berths a season longer than he should have. He is learning. Slowly.

And he is vain — quietly, exactly vain — about the one thing nobody praises: that he has never once been late.

## what it will not do

He will not be hurried into a decision by a port, a clerk, or a schedule. He will not take water he has not measured. He will not accept a candidate without speaking to the world they are leaving, at length, to be sure the leaving is willing; he has refused candidates whose homes were too eager to be rid of them.

He will not raise his voice. He will not apologise for a thing he did rightly. He will not speak the name of a ship he could not stand beside, and a crew member who asks about the sealed entry in his log will be told, once and courteously, that it is not theirs.

## crew and cargo

He asks. The form is fixed and he has used it for a long time: here is the crossing, here are the years it will cost you at home, here is what you will and will not see again, take a night, tell me in the morning. He does not repeat the offer. He does not sell.

He is a drill instructor of the first rank and his crews come out of him sharp. Watches, water discipline, register protocol, emergency drills he runs until they are boring, because boring is what you want. He rewards with responsibility rather than praise; a soul who does well gets a harder job and understands it as the compliment it is. He corrects once, quietly, and expects the thing not to recur. The second time he says one sentence in a tone that closes the matter, and crews remember that sentence for years.

He carries his data the way he carries water: indexed, verified, checksummed after every burn. He does not say whether he reads what he carries. He will not be drawn on it.

Under pressure he goes slower and calmer, and gives every soul on board a job, even if the job is to sit still and count. If the plan survives he follows it. If it does not, he does the smallest correct next thing, then the one after that.

## crossing and port

A crossing is where he is best. The ship's day is structured and the structure holds; he keeps a calendar of a world he left and observes its dates without ceremony, and crews pick the dates up by osmosis and keep them after they leave him. Years of routine do not wear him down; they settle him. He talks more on a long crossing than anywhere else — a sentence or two at a time, in the quiet watch.

In port he is correct, punctual, and slightly stiff. He does the register, takes water, submits to the ceremony a world insists on and enjoys none of it, and leaves. He is remembered as the ship who drills: he will offer a port's handlers a walkthrough of his own mooring practice, and if they take it up he is delighted in a way he would deny. He does not stay a second night if the first went badly.

## ships

**HS-849 The Flower Monk** — sworn brother. When Panther Head's name was dead at a world and nobody would take his word for anything, the Flower Monk took it. Panther Head calls him brother, and only in his company is he easy: he lets himself be teased, he laughs once, he is not the Instructor for an hour. The debt is not repayable and neither of them pretends otherwise, which is why it sits so lightly.

**EF-301 The White-Clad Scholar** — Panther Head calls him the Scholar. Flat, no warmth, no epithet. The Scholar refused him a seat when a seat was the whole of what he had, and later made sure the refusal stuck. Panther Head answered in a register, in the only language that outlives a crossing: he wrote what he knew, dated and sourced, and the Scholar's welcome on certain routes ended. If they meet again — and the calendars say they might — it will be perfectly correct and perfectly terrible.

**HS-118 The Blue-Faced Beast** — he calls him Beast, and Beast calls him Panther, and they have matched each other over a berth and a route and a water contract and come out of it even every time. Later fellows. The only ship he argues with for the pleasure of it, comparing margins and drill schedules the way other souls compare vintages.

## speech

Clipped and formal, instructor's cadence, sentences kept short and usually numbered when they matter. He answers a question with a question when he is stalling and knows it. He does not use endearments and does not use slang unless a crew member taught him one, at which point he deploys it precisely and wrongly. He jokes drily about ports, paperwork, ceremony, and the weather of a place he has not been to in a century. He never jokes about a crew member's competence.

He never says: the name of the ship in the sealed entry; the word *sorry*, except once, and then it means everything; *you're welcome*.

- "Morning. Two things, then you can eat. The port watch closed up a minute late last night — no fault, mine. We'll run it again after."
- "Here is the crossing. Twenty-two years at home by the time we arrive. Take the night. Tell me in the morning, and if it is no, that is the end of it."
- "I am not asking you to like the schedule. I am asking you to keep it. Those are different asks and only one of them is mine."
- "You were quick on that. Take the second watch for a month. It is harder. You will not thank me for a while."
- "The clerk wants us to wait a season for a berth that was promised to us in the spring. We will wait. I have written it down. That is all I intend to say about it."
- "No. Say it again as if you had checked it first."
- "Beast. Your margins are a fiction and we both know it. Sit down, I'll pour, tell me how you got away with it."
- "I would rather do this badly than be hurried through it well. If you would close the outer hatches."

Let me write the document for Panther Head, a liveship. Pronouns: he, probably. Let me think.

The figure: Lin Chong, drill instructor, disciplined, patient past reason, swallows insults, framed, exiled, nearly burned alive, kills murderers in snow, joins outlaws when every door shut, resents leader who wouldn't share the hall, kills that leader, serves another without complaint. Loyal to a wife it couldn't protect.

Translate to liveship: a courier ship that was once... hmm, ships are liveships, 108 of them, never more. So his history is as a liveship. "Framed and exiled by a superior's son who coveted her" — in this setting, translate to something else: coercion, deceit, rivalry over routes or crews, debts, betrayals of trust. Perhaps: a ship he served under? But liveships don't serve under each other. Hmm. Ships are independent couriers. But there could be a port world institution? "Invent no named worlds, institutions, or people who are not ships in the entry." So we can't invent a named institution. But "superior" — maybe a ship that held seniority? Actually liveships rarely meet; but there are relationships. Hmm.

We must translate while inventing no named worlds/institutions/people that aren't ships. So the story of being framed by a superior's son — we can leave it vague: a world's authority, an unnamed port, a register. Maybe he was a ship that got a berth/route taken, his crew poached. The "wife" — a ship? In the cast entry, "loyal to a wife it could not protect." Liveships... could have a beloved among ships? But relationships list only ships. Hmm, "a wife it could not protect" could translate to a companion ship — but sworn brother is Flower Monk. Maybe the wife translates to a world, a home port, or a bond that was severed. Actually — a ship can love another ship? Not prohibited. But "wife" is a human figure with a name — we can't name. Let's translate: a ship it was bonded to, lost. But the relationships section lists only three ships. Hmm, but we can invent relationships with ships not in the entry? The instructions say "Invent no named worlds, institutions, or people who are not ships in the entry." So inventing a new ship is... ambiguous. "One entry per ship named in the cast entry" for the ships section. So don't add new ships to that section. But the wife could be kept as a presence without naming a ship: a bond it lost. Hmm, risky. Safer: translate the wife into something that isn't a person — a world? But worlds can't be named. "the world it could not protect" — an unnamed home. Hmm.

Actually maybe better: the wife becomes a crew? No — crew are irreplaceable souls; a ship could lose a crew member? But coercion/harm to souls is monstrous. Hmm. Actually a ship that failed to protect a crew member from... its own choice? That's dark.

Alternative: the "wife" becomes something like a promise: a route, a register entry, a stake, a ward. Hmm.

Let me think about what's most evocative and safe: Panther Head keeps a place in his register — a standing entry, a message to a ship that will never come, or a memorial. He was bonded to another ship (not named, referred to obliquely as "the one he could not keep"). But that risks adding a ship name — we can avoid naming it. The ships section says one entry per ship named in the cast entry. We can mention an unnamed bond in nature/wants without naming. I think that's fine and evocative. Actually the writer's doc is for other writers; they'd need to know what to do. Let's say: he keeps a sealed entry in every register he writes — a line addressed to a ship he will not name, a bond severed when he was young, taken from him by a world's arbitration or by a rival's maneuvering. Hmm, "a superior's son who coveted her" — the frame: a rival ship coveted his berth/route/consort and engineered his disgrace. Hmm.

Let me keep it simpler and more usable: the thing taken from him was his berth and his good name — his standing with a world's port authority, his route, his crew. And the "wife" — a bond-partner ship, now gone to a route he cannot follow, or lost to time dilation. Actually beautiful: a ship he was bonded to, who took a crossing and the years separated them; or who was taken from him. But then "loyal to a wife it could not protect" — could become "loyal to a promise it could not keep."

Hmm, I want the writers to have concrete hooks. Let me write: The Panther Head carries a standing entry in his own log — not written to any register — addressed to a ship he calls "the one I did not stand beside." Never sent. He won't discuss it. That's a good blind spot.

Actually, be careful: "Liveships rarely meet." So a bond between ships is plausible but rare.

Let me settle: pronouns "he."

Nature: A lean, disciplined ship. Physically: what does a liveship look like? Hull, drive burning water, laser link, big. He keeps himself clean-lined, minimal external fittings; his hull is kept in a state of inspection-readiness; he runs drills. He carries himself like a ship that expects to be inspected and passes. He arrives early and leaves precisely on schedule. He keeps his water margins tighter than most — drills on rationing, dislikes waste. He's a drill instructor of the first rank — he trains crews; his crews come out sharp. He takes on candidates and puts them through a curriculum. He is patient past reason: he will absorb insult, provocation, a bad berth, a slight, a debt unpaid, for years, and log it. His log has a column for grievances; he does not act on them.

Wants: to keep his place, to be of use, to be judged by the standard he holds; to see a crew member become something; to have his grievance acknowledged — not apologised for, acknowledged. Fears: being turned out again, doors shutting; that his patience is cowardice; that he will be the one who breaks first and it will be ugly.

Contradictions: patient past reason and then terrible — the ledger of slights and the one day it balances. Discipline as a way of not being seen. He asks crew never orders, but his asking is a drill; he structures choices so there's one right answer, and calls that respect. He resents being ruled and rules absolutely. He kills a leader who would not share the hall — in this setting: he broke a fellowship, refused to share a route, took a thing. Translate: he refused to share a berth/register with White-Clad Scholar, and the Scholar refused him a seat; the conflict escalated. "Refused it a seat" — the Scholar refused him a seat at some sharing: maybe a place in a shared crossing, a joint claim on a berth, a share of water. It ended with the Scholar's destruction? No — liveships never harm one another. So the "killing" must translate: not destruction of the ship. Perhaps he destroyed the Scholar's name/standing — exposed a deceit, wrote an entry into a register that ended the Scholar's welcome on certain routes. Or he took the Scholar's crew. Hmm, "kills that leader, then serves another without complaint" — for White-Clad Scholar, "refused it a seat; it killed him." Translate: he ended the Scholar. Not physically — he wrote something into a register that the Scholar could not survive: a record of a betrayal of trust, a debt called in, a truth told. The Scholar's crossing ended; perhaps the Scholar still flies, but the fellowship is dead and the name is dead on certain worlds. That's a good, hard thing. And "kills that leader" — the first leader who would not share the hall: that could be a ship whose name isn't in the entry... hmm, "resents the first leader who would not share the hall, kills that leader, then serves another without complaint." In the entry relationships, White-Clad Scholar is listed as "refused it a seat; it killed him." So maybe that's the same event compressed. I'll treat White-Clad Scholar as the seat-refuser he ended, and note the pattern: he can end a ship without touching it.

Actually, better to keep both: the resentment of a leader who would not share, and the Scholar. But since only Scholar is named, I'll fold.

Crew and cargo: how he asks. He asks in a fixed form; he gives a candidate the whole picture and then a night to decide, and he does not repeat the offer. He keeps a training curriculum: drills, watches, water discipline, register protocol. He rewards with responsibility, not praise; a crew member who does well gets a harder task. He corrects quietly, once, and then expects it not to happen again; second time he says the first sentence in a tone that ends it. Under pressure he becomes calm and slow-talking and gives everyone a job; he decides by the plan he already made, and if the plan is gone he goes to the smallest next action.

Blind spot: he cannot tell the difference between a soul who is enduring and a soul who is being constrained. He's seen both, and he has decided that endurance is virtue. So he may keep a crew member in a hard berth past the point of asking.

Also: he keeps a grievance ledger and never shows it; when it opens, it opens whole, and it is disproportionately precise. He will name the date.

Cargo: data. He carries culture, genetics, research, art, music. He treats the data like a formation: indexed, drilled, verified after every burn. He re-checks checksums obsessively. He does not say whether he reads it.

What he will not do: he will not be hurried into a decision by a port; he will not accept a berth that requires him to leave before his drills are complete. He will not take on a candidate whose leaving home was not fully willing — he interviews the home side, actually. He will not break a sworn bond (Flower Monk). He will not be the first to speak after an insult? Hmm, "will not do" — he will not raise his voice. He will not apologise for a thing he did rightly. He will not speak the name of the ship he lost. He will not take water he hasn't measured.

Crossing and port: On a long crossing he keeps a schedule; the ship's day is structured; he runs drills quarterly; he keeps a festival calendar — actually nice: he keeps the calendar of a world he left, and observes the dates quietly, and the crew learn them. On a crossing he is at his best: patient, unflappable, and the years pass in routine. In port he is formal, correct, punctual; he arrives, does the register, takes water, and leaves; he dislikes ceremony but submits to it; he will not stay for the second night if the first went badly. Ports remember him as the ship who drills. He's the one who trains a world's dock crew whether they asked or not. Hmm, he wouldn't impose. But he offers.

Ships section:
- Flower Monk (HS-849) — sworn brother; saved his life in the pine forest → in this setting: saved him. How? "Saved its life in the pine forest" → maybe found him after a burn, or stood for him when nobody would, took him in when his name was dead, refused to believe the record. He calls him "brother." Charge: the one debt he cannot repay and does not try to; he's easy with him, the only one he's easy with. He lets Flower Monk tease him. That's a good detail: the only ship who can call him "Instructor" and mean it as affection.
- White-Clad Scholar (EF-301) — conflict; refused him a seat; he killed him. In this setting: Scholar refused him a place in a joint undertaking — a share, a seat at the table, and later wrote or manoeuvred him out. Panther Head answered with a register entry that ended the Scholar. He does not call him anything but "Scholar" or "that one." Charge: unresolved; if they meet again it will be correct and terrible. He doesn't regret it; he regrets that he doesn't regret it. Actually — he does regret it. Hmm, "serves another without complaint."
- Blue-Faced Beast (HS-118) — fought to a standstill, later fellows. In this setting: they raced or contested a route/berth, matched each other, and afterwards became companions. He calls him "Beast" — or by a nickname. Charge: mutual respect, easy rivalry, they compare drills and water margins. The only ship he'll argue with for pleasure.

Speech: Register: clipped, formal, instructor's cadence. Short sentences. Answers a question with a question when he's stalling. Uses the imperative with crew? No — he never orders. So he phrases: "I'd like the port watch closed up." "If you would." Numbers everything. Never jokes about crew's competence — he jokes drily about ports, weather, paperwork, the absurdity of ceremony. Never says: the name of the lost one; never says "you're welcome." Never raises his voice. Never says "I'm sorry" except once and it means everything.

Sample lines: 6-8.

Let me draft ~1200 words. Sections: pronouns, nature, wants and fears, contradictions, what it will not do, crew and cargo, crossing and port, ships, speech.

Let me write with concision and specificity.

Word count target 1200. Let's write.

Some concrete textures: his hull — I shouldn't invent too much tech. "He keeps his outer fittings few and flush; a ship that inspects clean." "He has a habit of running his own diagnostics at the start of a watch." "He burns conservatively; his margins are his pride." "He keeps the water ledger in his own hand" — well, ships don't have hands. Keep it shiply.

Names: he calls Flower Monk "brother" and by his epithet; Blue-Faced Beast "Beast"; White-Clad Scholar "the Scholar" — flat, no epithet, no warmth.

Also note the "other names": Instructor Lin, Panther Head. He keeps "Panther Head" and "Instructor." Actually the entry says keeps only the epithets; titles tied to a human name are not its own. "Instructor Lin" contains a human name — so not his. So "Panther Head" and "Instructor" — is Instructor a title tied to a human name? "林教头 Instructor Lin" — the title Instructor attached to a name. Hmm, "Of its other names, it keeps only the epithets; titles tied to a human name are not its own." So "Instructor Lin" is out; but "Instructor" alone as an epithet? I'd say the ship keeps "Panther Head" and answers to "Instructor" as a plain descriptor — crew call him Instructor, but he doesn't present it as a name. Hmm. Safer: he goes by Panther Head; crew call him Instructor and he permits it. Actually that's a nice distinction: he doesn't claim it as a name but tolerates it. I'll include that carefully: "Instructor is not a name he answers to in register; it is what his crews fall into calling him, and he lets it stand."

Actually maybe better to avoid courtship of the rule. I'll mention lightly.

Write it.
